cards.title: Zero-party vs first-party vs third-party data
cards.summary: Define the three data tiers and recognize that first-party tracking often misattributes the true source of a conversion.
cards.use_when: When deciding which customer data to collect and trust for store merchandising, acquisition channel decisions, or attribution reporting.
steps: Separate data into three tiers: zero-party (what the customer explicitly tells you, e.g., post-purchase surveys), first-party (what you track on your own site, e.g., purchase history, session data), and third-party (aggregated external data, e.g., credit-bureau-style sources like Experian).
Treat zero-party data as the priority for understanding the 'why' behind a purchase — it captures intent and discovery source that tracking cannot see.
Treat first-party tracking as necessary for behavior and funnel mechanics but unreliable for attribution because it frequently misattributes the real source of conversion.
Use third-party data only for enrichment and audience expansion, never as your ground truth for what drove a sale.
Cross-check first-party attribution claims against zero-party answers before shifting budget or merchandising based on either alone.
caveats: Zero-party data is self-reported and subject to recall error and survey framing bias.
First-party tracking is degraded by consent loss and tracking prevention, so discrepancies between platform and self-reported attribution are expected, not proof of error.

cards.title: Use post-purchase surveys to capture attribution truth
cards.summary: Run post-purchase surveys with tools like Fairing or Octane AI to surface the discovery source tracking misses.
cards.use_when: When platform attribution (e.g., a Google Ads dashboard claiming a sale) disagrees with what customers say, or when setting acquisition budget allocation.
steps: Deploy a post-purchase survey at the order-confirmation or thank-you step asking 'How did you hear about us?' with answer options that map to your real channel mix (including 'friend/family', podcast, influencer, etc.).
Use tools named in the source such as Fairing (formerly EnquireLabs) or Octane AI to collect and aggregate the responses; verify current features and pricing on each tool before committing.
Compare self-reported answers against platform-claimed conversions for the same period and channels.
Where the two diverge significantly, favor the self-reported signal for strategic channel decisions and note the platform number as a directional efficiency metric.
Keep the survey short and offer an incentive if completion is low; the goal is a usable sample, not perfection.
caveats: Self-reported attribution is recalled and approximate; a customer may name a channel they merely encountered last.
This source frames zero-party data as often conflicting with first-party attribution — the recommendation to prioritize qualitative feedback is the presenter's view, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Prioritize the 3% most loyal and 3% most dissatisfied customers
cards.summary: A source rule of thumb: mine qualitative feedback primarily from your most devoted and most unhappy customers.
cards.use_when: When gathering customer feedback for product development, PDP copy, or retention offers and you cannot survey the whole base.
steps: Identify the top ~3% most loyal customers (repeat purchasers, high LTV) and the bottom ~3% most dissatisfied (refunds, complaints, negative reviews) per the source's rule of thumb.
Interview or survey both groups directly — loyalty reveals what to double down on, dissatisfaction reveals fixable friction.
Apply loyal-customer insights to merchandising, bundles, and subscription/replenishment design.
Apply dissatisfied-customer insights to product-page expectation setting, sizing/description fixes, and post-purchase service.
Use the mid-base mainly for quantitative validation, not deep qualitative discovery.
caveats: The 3%/3% split is a source-specific heuristic, not a validated benchmark.
Extremes can be unrepresentative; pair with broader quantitative data before making large changes.

cards.title: Avoid HiPPO decision-making
cards.summary: The Highest Paid Person's Opinion can cherry-pick data to confirm biases instead of letting raw data drive strategy.
cards.use_when: When an executive or founder wants to change pricing, merchandising, or channel spend based on conviction rather than evidence.
steps: Name the risk explicitly: the source warns against HiPPO decision-making, where leaders use data selectively to confirm preconceived biases.
Before committing to a strategy change, ask what data would falsify the belief, not just what supports it.
Require an incrementality or holdout test (see separate card) before large budget shifts driven by opinion.
Separate the decision-maker's hypothesis from the metric that will judge it, and write both down.
Where conviction is strong but evidence is thin, run the test in a limited segment rather than across the whole store.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion; there are legitimate cases where founder intuition beats available data, especially at very small scale with low traffic.
Incrementality tests require enough volume to be meaningful.

cards.title: Distinguish compounding metrics from linear metrics
cards.summary: Some metrics compound over time (conversion rate, referral coefficient) while others scale linearly, so they deserve different investment logic.
cards.use_when: When allocating effort between acquisition, retention, and referral programs, or when explaining why a metric's improvement is worth more than it appears.
steps: Classify your key metrics: compounding metrics (e.g., conversion rate, referral coefficient) improve future results because their gains feed back into the system; linear metrics scale proportionally with spend.
For compounding metrics, accept that early improvements may look small but accumulate — protect and invest in them even when quarter-to-date impact is modest.
For linear metrics, judge purely on marginal cost and margin; there's no compounding upside to justify a loss-making spend.
Use this distinction to argue for CRO and referral program investment against a purely spend-based growth plan.
Track the compounding metrics over longer windows than you track linear ones.
caveats: Compounding effects take time to appear and are easy to under-measure in short reporting windows.
This framing is the presenter's, not an established financial formula.

cards.title: Reconcile platform attribution with self-reported attribution
cards.summary: Expect and plan for the gap between what ad platforms claim and what customers say drove the purchase.
cards.use_when: When Google Ads or a social platform reports conversions that zero-party survey data does not corroborate, and you must decide budget.
steps: Pull platform-attributed conversions for a channel for a defined window.
Pull post-purchase survey answers naming that channel for the same window.
Compute the gap and treat the platform number as directional, not exact — consent loss and tracking prevention cause platform numbers to miss or over-claim.
If a platform over-claims relative to self-reported attribution, avoid cutting it solely on the platform number until you test incrementality.
If self-reported attribution names channels the platform cannot see (word of mouth, podcasts, offline), preserve budget there even without a tracked conversion.
caveats: Neither number is ground truth; they measure different things (tracked touchpoints vs stated memory).
The source treats self-reported attribution as often the more honest signal, which is a stance, not a proven rule.

cards.title: Test incrementality instead of trusting attribution
cards.summary: Use holdout and incrementality tests to determine whether spend actually caused sales attribution claims.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to scale, cut, or keep a paid channel whose platform-reported ROAS may be inflated.
steps: Define the channel or tactic to test and the outcome metric (sales, new-customer count, contribution margin).
Create a holdout: pause or suppress exposure for a randomly selected segment or geography while keeping the rest live.
Measure the difference in outcomes between exposed and held-out groups over a sufficient window.
Compare the incremental lift to the platform-reported conversion volume; the gap is the over-claim.
Scale spend only where incremental lift justifies the cost, not where platform ROAS alone looks strong.
caveats: Requires enough volume and clean segmentation; small stores may lack the traffic for a reliable test.
The source raises incrementality as the corrective to HiPPO and misattribution but does not supply a formula or threshold here.

cards.title: Capture the 'why' behind quantitative results with qualitative tools
cards.summary: Use session and feedback tools like Hotjar alongside surveys to explain the reasons attribution numbers cannot.
cards.use_when: When checkout or PDP conversion is underperforming and you need the reason, not just the rate.
steps: Instrument qualitative capture alongside analytics: session recordings and heatmaps (source names Hotjar) to see where users hesitate, and surveys to hear why.
Pair each quantitative anomaly (a drop-off, a low-converting page) with a qualitative artifact (recording, survey verbatim) before proposing a fix.
Confirm tool fit on the current interface before setup, since features change.
Route the findings into concrete store changes: copy, layout, shipping messaging, or bundle structure.
Repeat after changes to see whether the stated reason was the real blocker.
caveats: Session recordings are samples and can over-weight unusual sessions; corroborate with surveys.
Tool names come from the source and should be verified for current capability.

input.text:
06-MEA / measurement and economics

Goes here. Whether any number can be trusted, and what the numbers mean. Event contracts, deduplication, match quality, attribution windows and restatement, profit and contribution formulas, landed cost, return rate, incrementality, consent, UTM integrity.

Not here.

Deciding whether a difference between two variants on a landing page is real -> 09-CRO

How to install a pixel -> 05-SET

Paid social creative formats -> 10-MCR

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Emphasizes the critical difference between quantitative and qualitative data collection in e-commerce, stressing that zero-party data (from surveys/conversations) often conflicts with first-party attribution data, and highlights the danger of "HiPPO" (Highest Paid Person's Opinion) decision-making ignoring incrementality tests. modules: [MEA] topics: [incrementality and holdouts, consent and tracking loss] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. incrementality and holdouts / prioritizing qualitative "zero-party" data (from post-purchase surveys and customer conversations) to uncover the "why" behind quantitative attribution data, noting that first-party tracking often misattributes the actual source of conversion. Using tools like Hotjar, Fairing (formerly EnquireLabs), and Octane AI to capture customer feedback. consent and tracking loss / adjusting to discrepancies between platform attribution (e.g., Google Ads claiming a sale) and self-reported attribution (e.g., a customer stating they heard about the brand from a friend).

Look for. The definitions of data tiers: Zero-party data (what the customer explicitly tells you, e.g., post-purchase surveys), First-party data (what you track directly on your site, e.g., purchase history), and Third-party data (aggregated external data, e.g., Experian). The rule of thumb for qualitative feedback: focus primarily on the 3% most loyal customers and the 3% most dissatisfied customers. The warning against "HiPPO" (Highest Paid Person's Opinion) decision-making, where executives use data selectively to confirm preconceived biases rather than letting raw data dictate strategy. The distinction between compounding metrics (e.g., conversion rate, referral coefficient) and linear metrics.

Skip. General prognostications about the future of AI replacing copywriters, customer service agents, and media buyers. Commentary on the future of the 4-hour workweek, web3, the gig economy, or the democratization of Shopify. Personal anecdotes about organizing e-commerce events or the speaker's own Twitter handle origin story.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 15 to 20.
